topics.topic: Calorific value and characteristics of a good fuel

subtopics.title: Classification of fuels and calorific value
subtopics.theory_md:
A **fuel** is a combustible substance that gives heat on burning. **Calorific value (CV)** is the heat liberated by complete combustion of unit mass (solids, liquids) or unit volume (gases) of the fuel.

- Units: cal/g, kcal/kg, kJ/kg, BTU/lb; gases kcal/m$^3$. $1\ \mathrm{kcal/kg} = 1\ \mathrm{cal/g} = 1.8\ \mathrm{BTU/lb}$.
- Classification: by state (solid, liquid, gas) and by origin: **primary** (natural: wood, coal, crude oil, natural gas) or **secondary** (derived: coke, petrol, producer gas, LPG).
subtopics.basics_md: Burning a fuel is a reaction that releases heat. CV is simply 'how much heat one kilogram gives', so a bigger CV means less fuel for the same job.
key_points: CV = heat from complete combustion of unit mass (or volume) of fuel
Units: cal/g = kcal/kg; 1 kcal/kg = 1.8 BTU/lb; gases kcal/m$^3$

subtopics.title: Gross and net calorific value
subtopics.theory_md:
Hydrogen in a fuel burns to steam: $\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$, so 1 part H gives 9 parts water.

- **GCV (HCV)**: products are cooled to room temperature, the steam condenses and its **latent heat is included**. The bomb calorimeter measures it.
- **NCV (LCV)**: products escape hot, so the latent heat is **lost**. It is the practical value.

$$\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587\ \text{cal/g}$$

$H$ = % hydrogen. If H = 0, NCV = GCV.
subtopics.basics_md: When wood burns you see steam. If that steam is let out, the heat locked in it is wasted. NCV is the heat you really get; GCV adds back what the steam would give if you cooled it.
key_points: GCV includes latent heat of condensed steam; NCV excludes it
NCV = GCV - 0.09 H x 587 (H in %, 587 cal/g latent heat)
1 part H gives 9 parts water, so water per g fuel = 0.09 H

subtopics.title: Characteristics of a good fuel
subtopics.theory_md:
A good fuel has:
1. **High calorific value**: less fuel to buy, store and carry.
2. **Moderate ignition temperature**: too low means fire hazard in storage; too high means hard to kindle.
3. **Low moisture**: moisture adds weight without heat and wastes heat in evaporating.
4. **Low ash** (non-combustible matter).
5. Moderate, controllable rate of combustion.
6. Harmless products (little $\mathrm{SO_2}$, CO, smoke).
7. Low cost, easy availability, easy storage and transport.
subtopics.basics_md: Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature a fuel must be heated to before it keeps burning on its own. Petrol catches at low temperature, wood needs much more.
key_points: High CV, low moisture, low ash

subtopics.title: Solid vs liquid vs gaseous fuels
subtopics.theory_md:

subtopics.title: Producer gas and water gas
subtopics.theory_md:
Both are made by passing a reactant over red-hot coke.

**Producer gas**: air (a little steam) over coke at about 1100 $^\circ$C. $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2 + C \rightarrow 2CO}$. Composition: CO 22-30%, $\mathrm{N_2}$ 50-56%, $\mathrm{H_2}$ 8-12%. CV about **1300 kcal/m$^3$**. Used for heating furnaces.

**Water gas**: steam over coke at about 1000 $^\circ$C. $\mathrm{C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2}$ (endothermic, so air blows alternate). Composition: CO about 41%, $\mathrm{H_2}$ about 51%, $\mathrm{N_2}$ about 4%. CV about **2800 kcal/m$^3$**; also a source of $\mathrm{H_2}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Producer gas is diluted by the nitrogen of the air used to make it; water gas is made with steam, so it has no such dilution.
key_points: Producer gas: air over red-hot coke, CO + N2 (over 50% N2), CV about 1300 kcal/m3
Water gas: steam over red-hot coke, CO + H2 (about 92%), CV about 2800 kcal/m3
Water gas is superior because it has little non-combustible N2

subtopics.title: Biogas (gobar gas)
subtopics.theory_md:
**Biogas** is made by **anaerobic digestion** (bacteria, no air) of cattle dung and plant or kitchen waste. Composition: $\mathrm{CH_4}$ 55-65%, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ 30-40%, traces of $\mathrm{H_2}$, $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$; CV about 5300 kcal/m$^3$.

Three stages: **hydrolysis**, **acid formation** (acetic acid, $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2}$), **methane formation** by methanogens: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH \rightarrow CH_4 + CO_2}$.

Uses: cooking, lighting, engines; spent slurry is manure.

subtopics.title: Construction and working of the bomb calorimeter
subtopics.theory_md:
A known mass of fuel is burnt in excess $\mathrm{O_2}$ in a closed bomb; heat is absorbed by water and calorimeter. Used for solid and non-volatile liquid fuels.

**Parts**: stainless-steel **bomb** with screw cap, $\mathrm{O_2}$ inlet valve and two electrodes; Ni/Pt **crucible** with fuel pellet; Mg **fuse wire**; copper **calorimeter** with water; **stirrer**; **Beckmann thermometer** (0.01 $^\circ$C); **air jacket and water jacket** against heat loss; 6 V battery.

**Working**: weigh 0.5-1 g pellet, fill bomb with $\mathrm{O_2}$ at about **25 atm**, immerse, note $t_1$, ignite, note maximum $t_2$.
subtopics.basics_md: It is a strong closed steel pot. The fuel burns inside it in pure oxygen and every bit of heat goes into the surrounding water, whose temperature rise we read.
key_points: Parts: steel bomb, crucible, fuse wire, calorimeter, stirrer, Beckmann thermometer, jackets
Bomb filled with O2 at about 25 atm; electric ignition by fuse wire
Heat of fuel absorbed by water + calorimeter; rise t2 - t1 noted

subtopics.title: Corrections and the calculation
subtopics.theory_md:
Heat from fuel = heat taken by water and calorimeter. $W$ = mass of water, $w$ = **water equivalent** of calorimeter (g), $x$ = mass of fuel.

With corrections:
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) - (t_A + t_F + t_T)}{x}$$
- **Cooling correction** $t_c$: heat lost on the way, so it is **added** to the rise (in $^\circ$C).
- **Fuse wire** $t_F$, **acid** $t_A$ ($\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ formed from S and N), **thread** $t_T$: extra heat not from the fuel, so **subtracted** (in cal).

Then $\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587$.
subtopics.basics_md: The thermometer reads the heat of everything that burned, not only the fuel. So we take away the heat of the fuse wire, thread and acid, and add back what leaked away.

subtopics.title: Why NCV is less than GCV, and which is easier to find
subtopics.theory_md:
In the bomb the products cool to room temperature, so the steam from the fuel's hydrogen **condenses** inside and gives up latent heat to the water. The bomb therefore measures **GCV** directly.

In furnaces, boilers and engines the flue gas leaves hot, so steam is never condensed and its latent heat (587 cal/g) is lost. The heat actually available is the **NCV**, so efficiencies are calculated on it.

NCV cannot be measured easily (the steam would have to be kept uncondensed), so it is **calculated**: $\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587$, needing %H from ultimate analysis.

subtopics.title: Procedure of proximate analysis
subtopics.theory_md:
Proximate analysis gives **moisture, volatile matter, ash and fixed carbon**, by heating and weighing only.

1. **Moisture**: about 1 g in a silica crucible, oven at **105-110 $^\circ$C for 1 h**. $\%M = \text{loss}/x \times 100$.
2. **Volatile matter**: dried residue, crucible **covered**, furnace **925 $\pm$ 20 $^\circ$C for 7 min**. $\%VM = \text{loss}/x \times 100$.
3. **Ash**: residue heated **uncovered** at **700-750 $^\circ$C** to constant weight. $\%\text{Ash} = \text{residue}/x \times 100$.
4. **Fixed carbon**: $100 - (\%M + \%VM + \%\text{Ash})$.

All percentages are on the **original** coal mass $x$.
subtopics.basics_md: Heat gently and water goes; heat hard with the lid on and gases go but carbon stays; heat open to air and carbon burns away, leaving ash.

Ash: uncovered, 700-750 C; fixed carbon by difference

subtopics.title: Numericals on proximate analysis
subtopics.theory_md:
Work stepwise on the **original mass** $x$:

$\%M = \dfrac{x - m_1}{x}\times 100$, where $m_1$ is the mass after 110 $^\circ$C.

$\%VM = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{x}\times 100$, where $m_2$ is the mass after the covered heating.

$\%\text{Ash} = \dfrac{m_3}{x}\times 100$, where $m_3$ is the final residue.

**Pulverized coal** is coal dried and ground to a fine powder (about 70-80% passes a **200-mesh** sieve) and blown with preheated air through burners into the furnace, where it burns in suspension almost like a gas.

**Cracking** breaks large, high-boiling hydrocarbons into smaller, low-boiling ones (alkanes and alkenes): $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_5H_{12} + C_5H_{10}}$. It raises the **yield and quality of petrol** from heavy oil and gives olefins for petrochemicals.

- **Liquid phase**: 475-530 $^\circ$C, 30-100 kg/cm$^2$; petrol ON about 65-70.
- **Vapour phase**: 600-650 $^\circ$C, 10-20 kg/cm$^2$; more olefins and gum.

Heavy oil is cracked over a catalyst (**artificial clay, zeolite or alumina-silica**) at **300-450 $^\circ$C**, **1-5 kg/cm$^2$**, through **carbocations**; chains rearrange to branched ones, so petrol has high octane number (about 80-90).

subtopics.title: Knocking in petrol and diesel engines
subtopics.theory_md:
**Petrol (SI) knock**: spark ignites the charge; at high compression the unburnt **end gas** forms peroxides and **self-ignites before the flame reaches it**. Result: metallic knock, power loss, overheating. Straight-chain alkanes knock most: **n-alkanes > branched > olefins > cycloalkanes > aromatics**.

**Diesel (CI) knock**: fuel injected into hot compressed air has an **ignition delay**; if the delay is long, fuel accumulates and burns at once. Fuels that ignite with difficulty (aromatics, branched) knock.

So petrol knock is **too early** ignition, diesel knock **too late** ignition.
subtopics.basics_md: Petrol should wait for the spark, but a bad petrol lights by itself too soon. Diesel should light itself quickly, but a bad diesel waits too long and then goes off all at once.

subtopics.title: Antiknocking agents: TEL and MTBE
subtopics.theory_md:
**Antiknock agents** are added in small amounts to petrol to raise its octane number.

**TEL**, $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4}$: breaks the radical chain.
1. $\mathrm{Pb(C_2H_5)_4 \rightarrow Pb + 4\,\dot{C}_2H_5}$.
2. Pb / PbO destroy peroxides and chain radicals, so combustion is smooth.

PbO would deposit in the engine, so **ethylene dibromide** (or ethyl bromide) is added as **scavenger**: $\mathrm{Pb + C_2H_4Br_2 \rightarrow PbBr_2 + C_2H_4}$; volatile $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$ leaves with the exhaust.

Lead is toxic and poisons catalytic converters, so **MTBE** is used in unleaded petrol.
subtopics.basics_md: TEL stops the chain that causes knocking. Its waste, lead, is cleared out by a bromine compound.
key_points: TEL raises ON by destroying peroxides and radicals (chain breaker)
Ethylene dibromide / ethyl bromide: scavenger forming volatile PbBr2
Lead is toxic and poisons catalytic converters; MTBE replaces it

subtopics.title: Acid correction and validity of data
subtopics.theory_md:
Some questions give GCV and ask for NCV and a **correction**. Rearrange:

$t_A = (W+w)(\Delta t + t_c) - t_F - t_T - x\cdot\mathrm{GCV}$.

Then **comment on validity**:
- $t_A$ must be **positive** and small (a few tens of cal).
- Heat absorbed by the calorimeter must equal $x \times \mathrm{GCV}$ plus corrections.
- NCV < GCV; composition adds to about 100%.

If these fail, the data are **inconsistent**.
subtopics.basics_md: If the water cannot have absorbed as much heat as the fuel should release, the numbers cannot all be true.

subtopics.title: Dulong's formula
subtopics.theory_md:
When no calorimeter data are given, estimate GCV from the ultimate analysis:
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{1}{100}\left[8080\,C + 34500\left(H - \frac{O}{8}\right) + 2240\,S\right]\ \text{kcal/kg}$$
with C, H, O, S in %. $O/8$ is the **available-hydrogen** correction: oxygen is already combined with hydrogen. N and ash give no heat. If %H is not given, take it **by difference** from 100. Then $\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H\times587$.
subtopics.basics_md: Each element gives its own heat: carbon 8080, free hydrogen 34500, sulphur 2240 kcal/kg. Hydrogen already tied up with oxygen gives no heat, hence O/8.
key_points: Available hydrogen = H - O/8
H by difference if not given: 100 - (C + O + N + S + ash)

subtopics.title: Air required: solid or liquid fuel (by mass)
subtopics.theory_md:
Air has **23% $\mathrm{O_2}$ by mass** (21% by volume). Per kg of fuel:

| Element | Reaction | $\mathrm{O_2}$ needed |
|---|---|---|
| C | $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$ | $\tfrac{32}{12}\,C$ |
| H | $\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$ | $8\,H$ |
| S | $\mathrm{S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2}$ | $S$ |

Subtract the O already in the fuel. $\text{Min air} = \dfrac{100}{23}\times(\text{net } O_2)$. Excess air multiplies the air by $(1+e)$. **Dry products** = $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{SO_2}$, excess $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$ (water excluded).
subtopics.basics_md: Work out how much oxygen each element needs, subtract the oxygen the fuel already has, and divide by the share of oxygen in air.
key_points: O2 needed: 32/12 C + 8 H + S - O (per kg)
Minimum air = (100/23) x net O2 (by mass)
Excess air = min air x (1 + e); excess O2 = e x net O2

subtopics.title: Air required: gaseous fuel (by volume)
subtopics.theory_md:
For gases, equal volumes hold equal moles, so use **volume**. Air has **21% $\mathrm{O_2}$ by volume**.

| Gas | Reaction | $\mathrm{O_2}$ per volume |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CH_4}$ | $\mathrm{CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O}$ | 2 |
| CO | $\mathrm{CO + \tfrac12O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$ | 0.5 |
| $\mathrm{H_2}$ | $\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$ | 0.5 |
| $\mathrm{H_2S}$ | $\mathrm{H_2S + \tfrac32O_2 \rightarrow SO_2 + H_2O}$ | 1.5 |

$\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$ need no $\mathrm{O_2}$. **If the composition is given by weight, first convert to volume (mole) %: divide each mass by its molar mass.** Min air $= \dfrac{100}{21}\times\mathrm{O_2}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Gas volumes follow mole ratios, so the coefficients in the balanced equation are directly the litres of oxygen per litre of gas.
key_points: Equal volumes = equal moles: O2 per volume from the balanced equation
Weight % must be converted to volume % by dividing by molar mass
Min air = (100/21) x O2; excess multiplies it
